payload.proof_nl:
Let S be a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m, where m>=2. For each r\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, let x_r be the least positive integer q such that qm+r\in S.

We first justify that each x_r is well-defined. Since S has finite complement in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}, for each fixed r the infinite set \{qm+r:q\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\} cannot be disjoint from S; hence there exists some positive q with qm+r\in S. By the well-ordering principle, there is a least such positive q, namely x_r.

Now fix arbitrary i,j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}.

We will use the defining minimality of the numbers x_r repeatedly: if t\in\{1,\dots,m-1\} and q>0 satisfy qm+t\in S, then necessarily x_t\le q.

Case 1: i+j<m.

By definition of x_i and x_j, we have
x_i m+i\in S \quad\text{and}\quad x_j m+j\in S.
Since S is closed under addition,
(x_i m+i)+(x_j m+j)=(x_i+x_j)m+(i+j)\in S.
Because i+j<m and i,j\ge 1, we have i+j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}. Thus the element above has the form qm+(i+j) with q=x_i+x_j>0. By the minimality property of x_{i+j}, it follows that
x_{i+j}\le x_i+x_j.
Equivalently,
x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j},
which is exactly the first required inequality.

Case 2: i+j>m.

Again,
(x_i m+i)+(x_j m+j)=(x_i+x_j)m+(i+j)\in S.
Since i+j>m, rewrite this as
(x_i+x_j+1)m+(i+j-m)\in S.
Also, because i,j\le m-1 and i+j>m, we have 1\le i+j-m\le m-2, so i+j-m\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}. Therefore, by the defining minimality of x_{i+j-m},
x_{i+j-m}\le x_i+x_j+1.
Equivalently,
x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m},
which is exactly the second required inequality.

Since i and j were arbitrary in \{1,\dots,m-1\}, both assertions hold for all such i,j. This proves the lemma.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer with m ≥ 2
g is an integer with g ≥ 0
g + 1 is therefore an integer with g + 1 ≥ 1 (so the genus parameter remains in the intended nonnegative-integer regime)
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all integers m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0, letting N(m,g) be the number of numerical semigroups having multiplicity m and genus g, we have N(m,g) ≤ N(m,g+1).

domain_restrictions: S is closed under addition: ∀a,b ∈ S, a+b ∈ S
S has finite complement in Z_{≥0} (i.e., Z_{≥0} \ S is finite)
m is the least positive element of S: m ∈ S, m>0, and ∀t ∈ Z with 0 < t < m, t ∉ S
q ranges over integers in Z_{>0} when defining x_r
x_r is defined as a least positive integer q satisfying q·m + r ∈ S
Case split: inequalities are asserted only for i+j < m and for i+j > m; the case i+j = m is not specified
In the first inequality, i+j < m implies i+j ∈ {1,...,m-1}, so x_{i+j} is among the defined indices
In the second inequality, i+j > m implies i+j-m ∈ {1,...,m-1}, so x_{i+j-m} is among the defined indices
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let S be a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m≥2. For each r ∈ {1,...,m-1}, let x_r be the least q ∈ Z_{>0} such that q m + r ∈ S. Then for all i,j ∈ {1,...,m-1}: (i+j < m ⇒ x_i + x_j ≥ x_{i+j}) and (i+j > m ⇒ x_i + x_j + 1 ≥ x_{i+j-m}). No inequality is claimed for i+j = m.

For all i,j ∈ {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then ...; if i + j > m then ...

payload.statement_nl: Let S be a numerical semigroup, meaning a subset S of the nonnegative integers that contains 0, is closed under addition, and has finite complement. Assume its multiplicity is m, meaning m >= 2 is the least positive element of S. For each r in {1,...,m-1}, let x_r be the least positive integer q such that q m + r belongs to S. Then for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}.

detailed_findings.finding: Existence and well-definedness of x_r are correctly justified from the finite-complement property and well-ordering.
Case i+j<m is proved correctly by closure under addition and minimality of x_{i+j}.
Case i+j>m is proved correctly after rewriting the sum with residue i+j-m and applying minimality of x_{i+j-m}.
No semantic drift from the lemma sketch or the root theorem role: this is exactly the standard step showing the Apéry/Kunz coordinates satisfy the Kunz inequalities.

result_payload.reason: The proof correctly establishes existence of each x_r using finite complement of a numerical semigroup, then proves both Kunz-type inequalities by adding the defining semigroup elements and invoking minimality of the relevant x-index. The argument matches the stated lemma exactly, including the intended omission of the i+j=m case.
